claims.claim: Consumer protection is the set of laws and government agencies that guard buyers against unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices in the marketplace (working definition, built from FTC and CFPB descriptions).
In the United States, the FTC is the federal agency that enforces consumer protection law across the economy, targeting deceptive and unfair business practices.

In the United States, the CFPB enforces federal consumer financial law and oversees consumer financial products — bank accounts, credit cards, mortgages, and loans — so their markets are transparent, fair, and competitive.
Under U.S. rules, advertising claims must be truthful, cannot be deceptive or unfair, and must be evidence-based (the honest-advertising right).
Billing errors, such as a charge for something never bought, can be disputed with the company; disputing charges with the card issuer is part of fair-billing protection.
Financial institutions must explain their information-sharing practices to their customers and safeguard sensitive data (the privacy-of-financial-data right).

The general complaint path: try the company first; if that fails, file with the agency; the agency reviews and routes the complaint to the company, which responds — companies generally respond within about 15 days in the CFPB process; the agency uses complaint patterns to spot marketplace problems.

The FTC's fraud-reporting portal is ReportFraud.ftc.gov; the CFPB accepts complaints about financial products such as checking and savings accounts, credit cards, credit reports, mortgages, and loans.
Mortgages carry required disclosures: lenders give a Loan Estimate early in the process, and it is illegal for lenders to deliberately underestimate the costs on it.

Credit cards and loans carry required disclosures of key terms — rates, fees, and payment obligations (credit-card terms; TILA disclosures for loans) — so the costs of borrowing are knowable before the deal.
Consumer protection is a safety net, not a seatbelt: it makes prices, risks, and terms clear upfront and penalizes unfair practices, but it does not guarantee a good outcome for every decision.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which agency handles a given problem is not always obvious: the FTC covers the whole marketplace and the CFPB covers financial products, and complaints may be routed between agencies.
positions: FTC is the economy-wide consumer protection agency (FTC About page)
CFPB is the consumer-financial-products agency and takes financial-product complaints (CFPB bureau and complaint pages)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names both agencies with one line each, states the general split (FTC = whole marketplace; CFPB = financial products), and describes the general complaint process without promising a specific outcome for any agency.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What happens after a complaint is filed differs by agency and case; there is no universal promise of refund or resolution.
positions: CFPB routes complaints to companies, which generally respond in about 15 days, with 60 days in some cases (CFPB complaint page)
FTC reporting feeds pattern-spotting and enforcement; no individual outcome is promised (FTC reporting guidance)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the CFPB's general timeline as 'generally within about 15 days' and the honest note that a complaint does not guarantee a personal payout.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Disclosure documents vary by product, so no single document is universal.
positions: Mortgages use the Loan Estimate early in the process (CFPB)
Credit cards state rates and fees in card disclosures (CFPB credit-card hub)
Loans carry TILA disclosures of credit costs (CFPB)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the disclosure for each product in one line and does not generalize a single document across all products.

sourceRecords.title: About the FTC
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. States the FTC enforces federal competition and consumer protection laws that prevent anticompetitive, deceptive, and unfair business practices, and that consumer advice resources teach consumers their rights. Supports the working definition and the FTC one-line role. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: The CFPB
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. States the CFPB implements and enforces federal consumer financial law, ensures markets for consumer financial products are transparent, fair, and competitive, was created as a single point of accountability for protecting consumers in the financial marketplace, roots out unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices, and takes consumer complaints. Supports the CFPB role, the complaint-taking claim, and the honest framing (terms clear upfront so consumers can comparison shop).

sourceRecords.title: Submit a complaint
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Describes the complaint process: try the company first; include key facts, dates, amounts, and documents; the CFPB forwards the complaint to the company and asks for a response; companies generally respond within 15 days, with 60 days in some cases; complaints are shared with other agencies when they are better able to assist; data is published in the Consumer Complaint Database without information that directly identifies the consumer. Supports the complaint-process claims. No legal advice given.

sourceRecords.title: What To Do if You Were Scammed
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Consumer Advice
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. States that scams are reported to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and describes first steps after being scammed. Cited only for the general fact that ReportFraud.ftc.gov is the FTC's reporting portal; the lesson keeps scam details out of scope (sibling topic financial-scams).

sourceRecords.title: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. States the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires financial institutions to explain their information-sharing practices to their customers and to safeguard sensitive data, and that customers must be notified about what is collected, who it is shared with, and how it is protected. Supports the privacy-of-financial-data right, stated generally; no statutory detail or legal advice.

sourceRecords.title: Advertising and Marketing (business guidance)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. States that under the law, claims in advertisements must be truthful, cannot be deceptive or unfair, and must be evidence-based. Supports the honest-advertising right. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Can my final mortgage costs increase from what was on my Loan Estimate? (Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Confirms the Loan Estimate as a mortgage disclosure document and states it is illegal for lenders to deliberately underestimate the costs on it, while some costs can change under limited circumstances (change-in-circumstances). Supports the mortgage-disclosure claim; the lesson uses only the general disclosure point, not the exceptions detail.
